title: An irregular island
caption: Dwarf galaxy NGC 5264, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 5264 · constellation Hydra · about 15 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys captured the glow of distant stars in NGC 5264, a dwarf galaxy with an irregular shape and knots of blue star formation. It lies just over 15 million light-years away in Hydra, the Sea Serpent.

Dwarf galaxies like this one usually hold around a billion stars, only one per cent of the number in the Milky Way. They are generally found orbiting larger galaxies, and they are thought to form from material left over when their bigger relatives came together in a messy process.

Unlike the more common spiral and elliptical galaxies, NGC 5264 has no neat shape. Astronomers believe it was bent this way by gravitational encounters with other nearby galaxies. Those past close passes also set off new generations of star formation, and the young stars that resulted now shine in bright shades of blue across the galaxy.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.22 x 3.31 arcminutes) and distance (15 million light years), the frame spans roughly 14,000 × 14,000 light-years. Its light set out about 15 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines visible and near-infrared light captured by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the long exposure gathers far more light than an eye could.
